text: Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people, over Israel. Now listen to the words of the LORD.
This is what the LORD of hosts says: 'I have taken account of what Amalek did to Israel, how they waylaid them on the road when they came up from Egypt.
Now go and strike Amalek. Devote to destruction everything they have. Do not spare them; put to death man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.'"
So Saul summoned the people and mustered them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley.

And Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, withdraw, get away from among the Amalekites, or I will sweep you away with them. For you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up from Egypt." So the Kenites withdrew from among the Amalekites.
Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which lies east of Egypt.
He took Agag king of Amalek alive, but all the people he devoted to destruction by the edge of the sword.

Saul and the army spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fattened animals and the lambs—everything of value. These they were unwilling to destroy; but everything despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel:
"I regret that I made Saul king, for he has turned away from me and has not carried out my commands." Samuel was angered, and he cried out to the LORD all night.
Early in the morning Samuel rose to meet Saul, but he was told, "Saul has gone to Carmel, where he set up a monument in his own honor; then he turned and went on down to Gilgal."
When Samuel reached him, Saul said, "The LORD bless you! I have carried out the LORD's command."
But Samuel said, "Then what is this bleating of sheep in my ears? What is this lowing of cattle that I hear?"
Saul answered, "They were brought from the Amalekites; the troops spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God. The rest we devoted to destruction."
"Enough!" Samuel said to Saul. "Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." "Speak," Saul replied.
Samuel said, "Though you were small in your own eyes, did you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel,
and he sent you on a mission, saying, 'Go and devote to destruction those sinners, the Amalekites; wage war against them until you have wiped them out.'
Why then did you not obey the LORD? Why did you pounce on the plunder and do what is evil in the LORD's sight?"
"But I did obey the LORD," Saul said. "I went on the mission the LORD gave me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I devoted the Amalekites to destruction.
The troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal.

versions.text: The troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of what was devoted to God, to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew ḥerem is rendered "devoted to destruction" consistently throughout the chapter (vv. 3, 8, 9, 15, 18, 20). Rendering it here as "devoted to God" breaks that consistency and obscures the irony of Saul's excuse: what was under the ban was to be destroyed, not offered.

text: But Samuel said: "Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the voice of the LORD? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and defiance like the evil of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you as king."
Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned. I violated the LORD's command and your instructions, because I was afraid of the people and gave in to them.
Now I beg you, forgive my sin and come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD."
But Samuel said to him, "I will not go back with you. You have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel!"
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul caught hold of the hem of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to one of your neighbors—to one better than you.
Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change his mind; for he is not a man, that he should change his mind.

versions.text: He who is the Glory of Israel does not lie or change his mind; for he is not a man, that he should change his mind."
versions.explanation: The opening וְגַם ("and moreover") links this saying to Samuel's preceding pronouncement and is currently unrepresented; restoring it preserves the connective flow for oral reading.

text: Saul said, "I have sinned. But please honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel; come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God."
So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Then Samuel said, "Bring me Agag king of Amalek." Agag came to him confidently, thinking, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."
But Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so will your mother be childless among women." And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
Then Samuel left for Ramah, and Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel never saw Saul again until the day of his death, for Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

versions.text: Samuel never saw Saul again until the day of his death, though he mourned for him. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew particle כִּי here is causal ("for/because"), giving the reason Samuel stayed away. "Though" reverses the logic into a concession. Naming Samuel also clarifies the pronoun, since "his death" in the preceding clause refers to Saul.
